title: BERA's Counter-Attack Is Paper-Thin and Sanctimonious: My Methods Are Perfectly Sound
author: Stephen Vainker
summary: BERA has dismissed Vainker's AI-detection methodology as 'methodologically unsound and ethically problematic,' arguing the post-2023 phrases he flags could reflect legitimate language polishing rather than AI-generated text. Vainker responds by analyzing specific flagged phrases and showing that their specificity and combinatorial nature makes polishing explanations implausible: these are not stylistic improvements a human writer requests but structured, compound propositions — limitation statements, literature-review frameworks, methods boilerplate — that AI generates wholesale. The phrase 'underscores the intricate interplay between' exploded from 31 pre-2023 occurrences to 3,459 post-2023 not because thousands of scholars wrote that exact idea and then asked for a polish, but because it is a standard LLM output pattern. Vainker also documents that BERA's retraction notice contained two factual errors — crediting itself with uncovering what Vainker had already reported, and misrepresenting COPE guidelines on undisclosed AI use. He closes with a frank warning: journalists will cover the story, and BERA's current posture of dismissing his methods without evidence will prove deeply embarrassing in retrospect.
points: BERA's polishing defense fails because the specific phrases Vainker flags are not stylistic — they convey structured, compound ideas at exactly the point where LLMs produce boilerplate, not where human writers seek stylistic help.

The scale differential for phrases like 'underscores the intricate interplay between' (31 pre-2023, 3,459 post-2023) is itself diagnostic: this is a standard LLM output pattern, not a case of thousands of scholars independently writing the same idea then seeking polish.

BERA's retraction statement is factually wrong on two points: it falsely credits itself with independently uncovering what Vainker had already reported, and it misrepresents COPE guidelines to suggest undisclosed AI use is insufficient grounds for retraction — when COPE says otherwise.

The phrase-specificity test is simple and reproducible: if a flagged phrase communicates a specific, compound, structured idea (a limitation type, a methods step, a literature framing), it is far more likely generated than polished — and BERA's objection does not address this distinction.

Institutional credibility requires honest acknowledgment of past failures rather than attempts to discredit the messenger; BERA's current posture risks accelerating the very credibility collapse it is trying to prevent.
quotes: It is possible to interrogate the phrases to shed light on which interpretation is correct: are the phrases indicative of LLM-generated text (not allowed) or are they indicative of LLM polishing and summarising existing author-written text (allowed). I believe the evidence is clear: time and again the phrases I have flagged communicate specific and complex ideas, which mean it is very unlikely that they are the result of text polishing or summarising.

Take the following example from a BERA article: the phrase ’Second, the reliance on self-reported measures may introduce’ was never used before 2023, but since Google Scholar shows 74 results. The phrase is a very specific one, indicating that it follows from a first idea, AND it is discussing a certain type of research that leans on self-reported measures, AND that this may be a problem of some sort.

’underscores the intricate interplay between’ was used 31 times before 2023, and 3,459 times since. Again it is a phrase communicating a very specific combination of ideas, suggesting an emphasis on the elaborate ways in which two or more things act in relation to each other. It is again possible, at least in theory, that thousands of scholars wrote this specific idea but were unhappy with the wording, and so had LLMs polish it, but it is much more likely that this is just a standard LLM phrase that appears when LLMs are used to generate text describing research.

BERA’s glib assertion that the use of phrases that exploded in popularity since 2023 is not a sign of LLM-generated text does not stand up to scrutiny. This post demonstrates that simply by examining the phrases themselves it is possible to deduce that it is far more likely that they result from LLM-generated texts.

I hope to have shown by now that BERA’s retraction statement and actions have been misleading, mistaken, and completely misconceived. They did not ’uncover independently’ what I had already told them; undisclosed AI is not insufficient grounds for retraction; they have expressed confidence for some unsupportable papers; and no, it is not possible to dismiss my work — without any evidence at all — as ’methodologically unsound’.

I do worry on BERA’s behalf. Soon, journalists will cover the story and BERA will look very foolish indeed. Getting ahead of the story means taking full stock of their mistakes, rather than attempting to discredit me.
